passages.t: Wisdom calls at the city gates
passages.happening:
‘Does not wisdom call out, and understanding raise her voice?’ (verse 1). She stands on the heights by the road, at the crossroads and beside the city gates, and she calls: “To you, O men, I call out, and my cry is to the sons of men” (verse 4). “O simple ones, learn to be shrewd; O fools, gain understanding” (verse 5).

Everything she says is true and straight. ‘Receive my instruction instead of silver, and knowledge rather than pure gold’ (verse 10), ‘For wisdom is more precious than rubies’ (verse 11).

Then she speaks of herself. ‘To fear the LORD is to hate evil; I hate arrogant pride, evil conduct, and perverse speech’ (verse 13). ‘By me kings reign, and rulers enact just laws’ (verse 15). ‘I love those who love me, and those who seek me early shall find me’ (verse 17). Riches and honor are with her, and her fruit is better than gold (verses 18-19). She walks in the paths of justice and fills the storehouses of those who love her (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 7 ended with a woman whose house was the road to death, met at a dark corner. Chapter 8 answers with Wisdom, who calls in full daylight from the busiest places in town: the heights over the road, the crossroads, the gates where elders judged, traders met and travelers passed. Her voice is public, and it is for everyone, from the simple to all the sons of men.

Silver, gold and rubies were the most prized goods of the ancient economy. Wisdom says her gifts are worth more.

The idea that kings rule by wisdom was shared across the ancient Near East, where kings claimed wisdom as a gift of the gods and the ground of just rule. Solomon's prayer for wisdom to govern fits that picture, and Proverbs roots it in the LORD. Wisdom is not a skill that can be separated from goodness: to fear the LORD is to hate evil, pride and twisted speech.
passages.later: When Solomon judged wisely, ‘they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice’ (1 Kings 3:28). The psalm says the same of God's word as Wisdom says of herself: ‘They are more precious than gold, than much pure gold’ (Psalm 19:10). And Isaiah calls, ‘Seek the LORD while He may be found’ (Isaiah 55:6).
passages.asks: Wisdom calls in the busiest places, and she says she can be found by anyone who seeks her. Ask where you look for guidance first, and whether you seek her early or only when trouble comes. And ask whether your idea of wisdom includes hating pride and twisted speech, as hers does.

passages.t: Beside God before the world began
passages.happening:
Now Wisdom tells of her beginning. ‘The LORD created me as His first course, before His works of old’ (verse 22). ‘From everlasting I was established, from the beginning, before the earth began’ (verse 23). Before there were deep waters or springs, before the mountains and hills, she was brought forth (verses 24-25).

‘I was there when He established the heavens, when He inscribed a circle on the face of the deep’ (verse 27), when he set the clouds above and set a boundary for the sea, ‘when He marked out the foundations of the earth’ (verse 29).

“Then I was a skilled craftsman at His side, and His delight day by day, rejoicing always in His presence. I was rejoicing in His whole world, delighting together in the sons of men” (verses 30-31).
passages.hearers:
This poem is the high point of the book's opening chapters. Wisdom here is a personification, a quality of God given a voice and presented as a person, a common way of speaking in Hebrew poetry. The poem says that God made the world wisely, so that wisdom runs through the grain of creation. To live wisely is to live in step with how the world was made.

The poem carries the reader backward, before the mountains and seas, and then forward through the making of the world. First is the word reshit, the word that opens Genesis: in the beginning. Wisdom was the first of God's ways, there before any of his works.

The picture of the world is the ancient one: deep waters, springs, a circle drawn on the face of the deep, perhaps the horizon or the sky over the waters, and a boundary set for the sea. The sea was seen as a restless power only God could hold back. Wisdom was present at each step, not as a rival power but as God's delight.

Skilled craftsman translates amon, a rare word whose meaning is debated. Some read master worker, a partner in God's making. Others, from a word meaning to nurse, read little child or darling, a child playing in God's presence. Others read faithfully or constantly. Each reading fits the joy of the passage.
passages.later:
The poem reaches back to the Bible's first words: ‘In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth’ (Genesis 1:1). Job hears God speak of the same boundary for the sea: ‘You may come this far, but no farther’ (Job 38:11).

The New Testament speaks of Christ in language close to this chapter. ‘Through Him all things were made’ (John 1:3), and ‘He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together’ (Colossians 1:17). The picture of Wisdom at creation shaped how the apostles spoke of Christ as the one through whom all things were made, though the chapter itself is a poetic personification, not a prophecy.
passages.hard:
If Wisdom in Proverbs 8 is Christ, does verse 22 mean the Son was created?

This was exactly the argument of the fourth century AD. Arius argued from the Greek translation of verse 22, which says the Lord ‘created’ wisdom, that the Son was the first and highest of God's creatures. Several answers, then and now, carry weight.

First, the Hebrew verb, qanah, more often means to acquire or possess than to create, and translations still differ: created, possessed, brought forth. Verses 24 and 25 speak of wisdom being ‘brought forth’, birth language rather than making language.

Second, the chapter is poetry that personifies God's own wisdom. God was never without wisdom, so speaking of wisdom's beginning is a poetic way of saying that wisdom was there before anything else.

Third, the church's confession that the Son is eternal and not made rests on the New Testament's own direct teaching (John 1:1; Colossians 1:15-20; Hebrews 1), not on reading every detail of Proverbs 8 as a description of him. Athanasius and the other defenders of the faith confessed at Nicaea answered Arius in several ways.

Many Christian readers see Proverbs 8 as background that the New Testament's picture of Christ fills and goes beyond. Some older interpreters read it more directly of the Son. Both reject the Arian conclusion.
passages.asks: Wisdom was God's delight at the making of the world, and she delighted in people. Ask what it would change to believe the world was made wisely and with joy. And ask where you could look at creation this week and see that wisdom.

passages.happening:
‘Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways’ (verse 32). ‘Listen to instruction and be wise; do not ignore it’ (verse 33).

‘Blessed is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my doors, waiting at the posts of my doorway’ (verse 34). ‘For whoever finds me finds life and obtains the favor of the LORD’ (verse 35). The speech ends with a stark contrast: ‘But he who fails to find me harms himself; all who hate me love death’ (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
After the poem of creation, Wisdom turns back to her hearers. The same Wisdom who was at God's side when the world was made now waits at a doorway, and she promises life to anyone who will listen.

The picture of watching daily at her doors is the picture of someone eager to learn, waiting each morning for the door to open. Wisdom is not found once and then put away. She is sought day by day.

The chapter ends where the book always does: two ways. To find wisdom is to find life and the LORD's favor. To miss her is to wound oneself, on the road chapter 7 described.
passages.later: The psalms describe the same daily waiting on God's word: ‘Blessed are those who keep His testimonies and seek Him with all their heart’ (Psalm 119:2). And the next chapter turns Wisdom's invitation into a feast (Proverbs 9:1-6).
passages.asks: Wisdom's hearers wait at her door every day. Ask what daily habit could put you at that doorway. And ask whether there is some part of your life where you are, as the verse says, harming yourself by refusing to listen.
